titleStmt.title: Interview with Vernon A. Spencer, Undated
titleStmt.author: Sidney Halma

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Vernon A. Spencer was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Mr. Spencer, tell us a little bit about your background. Were you born in Catawba County?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I was born and raised in Catawba County, right here where this house set on. The old home place is right below here.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Tell us who your parents were.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: John A. Spencer and Sarah Little Spencer.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what year were you born?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Tell us about your family. Did you have brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I had one brother and three sisters.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Where did you fit into the family?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I was the next to the last.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. You were the baby boy of the family?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, there weren't but two boys that were born.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: How did your parents make a living?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Farming and railroad.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Tell us about what kind of farming did they do, what kind of crops did they raise and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We had two main crops--or three. Cotton was number one for a few dollars during the depression, and then wheat and soybean and grain and corn as in the grain family.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, your wheat, did you ever sell any of your wheat to Murray's Mill for grinding up there?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you deal with Lloyd Murray?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, Lloyd.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And Ernest?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. He's heavyset.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, tell us about how your family was involved with railroading.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, my dad worked the railroad, and then we still had the farm going, us kids, and then we'd hire a little help periodically gathering crops mainly and then putting the crops in the ground.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What kind of work did he do at the railroad?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: He was a sawer. He was the head sawer for Asheville division, ran a sawmill.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Catawba.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. Elementary school?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, started there and finished there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And did you go through high school?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes. Eleven grades in those days.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Eleven grades. That's right. And when you graduated from the eleventh grade, then what did you do?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Went to the Navy. Well, I worked about 11 months in the hosiery mill after I graduated, but I went to enlist in the Navy, myself and my friend. And the closest recruiting place we had then was in Charlotte.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Who was your friend that you enlisted with?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: O. D. Copeland.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Was he a classmate of yours?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, he was a dropout.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, he was a dropout?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I don't remember, ninth or tenth grade.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Not everybody finished school in those times.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, right. A lot of them dropped out in the seventh grade.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Were you drafted at some point in time or expected to get drafted?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, no. When I graduated from school, I was 16, when we graduated in May.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You were 16 years old?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You were too young?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, but then the next month I turned 17, and the Navy would accept you at 17 years old with a parent, one parent, and two reputable residents in your area, you know, to recommend you, sign for you. And then the Navy had a program then that when you became 21, you automatically got credit for four years of service. In other words, I got a little extra time there on my retirement that I didn't have to serve.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But you came in at 17?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And your father signed for you?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, my mother.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And then you had two others. Who were the others?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: John Phillip Coulter.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: The store owner?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, and Dr. Fred.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Dr. Fred Long?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Dr. Fred Long.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: With the cigars?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, and I took up after him.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You took up his cigars also?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes. He used to pick me up when I was just a little youngster on the road going by here, and we'd go to what was called Catfish. He picked me up once in a while to ride with him in his car just to take me for a ride. For some reason he took a liking to me. Anyway, those cigars he would smoke smelled awfully good.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Were they Cuban cigars. I expect them Cuban cigars?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: His were. But then later a cousin and I, we would try one out once in a while. But they were cheap ones, King Edwards.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Your folks were okay with you going into the Navy?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Your folks were okay with you enlisting in the Navy? Your family was okay? They didn't mind you going into the Navy?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: My dad didn't want me to go.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: He wanted you to stay on the farm?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, that plus I guess he was a little bit on the psychic side. He saw a lot of this scrap iron being shipped west going to Japan. And he told me why he wouldn't sign it. He says, "We're going to be at war with them Japs one of these days." He was so right.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But your mother said--

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She signed.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: She said it would be a good education for you?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. She signed for me.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: All right. Now, you are all signed up. So you had to go for your physical?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, see, when you get to a recruiting office, they give you a minor, you can call it, I guess, physical.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That was in Charlotte?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. But later if you pass that, then you got this little mental exam, and you got to pass that. Copeland and I both passed them, but there was a waiting list. The recruiter could just take so many men a quarter. Well, I was either 42nd or 43rd, and he was the other one.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you had to wait for the next one?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, this was in August when we were there. So we had a job in this little old mill, boarding socks. And come Christmastime, well, he told me--

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Which mill was that? Sidney Yount Mill?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, the one over here, it was Lylerly.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Lylerly?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Hosiery mill. And W. R. Keith was the superintendent of it. And then Norma Yount, well, she knew him. He was in charge of the warp room. He was my boss and Copeland's. But anyway we didn't know any of them. We thought maybe the recruiter had forgotten us about being down there. He told us when we left, after we took that little physical and little mental exam, that he would send us a card when to come in. Well, it was getting close to Christmas.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You hadn't heard from him?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We hadn't heard from him. So I asked Copeland about it, "Do you think we ought to go down and check with that recruiter?" So we went down there, and we went in the office. He started laughing. He said, "I got your cards here on my desk." So that was it then. They sent us from there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What time period are we talking about now?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: January. Well, we was there in December. But we didn't go to Raleigh until February.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Of '41 then?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, 1941. But in Raleigh, see, that's when you take your full physical and mental exam.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You boarded the train? Or did you take the bus out of Newton?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: The train from Raleigh to Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You boarded the train in Catawba then?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You didn't leave from Charlotte, did you?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, we did.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You left from Charlotte.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, because he had another young man there. You know, like I say, he had a quota, and he called some other men in. I think there was one from Shelby, a Walker, but I can't remember the other one. But anyway they put us on a train in Charlotte.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you went then to Raleigh?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: By train?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what happened in Raleigh?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, they gave us a full physical, a full exam. After that we stayed overnight. And after that they put us on a train headed for Norfolk. They had a group on there from different parts of the state.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That was a troop train, I guess.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What happened when you landed at Norfolk?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Went to the--well, we went to the recruit, where you started being placed in groups, you know, for your training.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Your orientation, I guess, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, yeah. And then you put so many men in a platoon. In ours there were 63, the one I was in.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: The platoon. And you began basic training?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, twelve weeks.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Twelve weeks. Tell us what basic training consisted of.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, to start with, you learned how to march. And then later you moved into the drill field.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Initially you had wooden rifles or real?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, real rifles.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You had real rifles right from the start?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: But they were fixed to where you couldn't--

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you couldn't move them around?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. But they would be the same weight.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Right. To get used to handling them?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Then, of course, you got training in that too, but that came a little later.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So first marching?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: And then the next step in it was working in the drill field like you would be with a lineman group. They had these old Browning machine guns mounted on two wheels, and there was an air crew. You had to know how to pull it, how to set it up and shoot it and so forth.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, when you initially came, they put everybody together. And when did your specialized training begin?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I don't think you could call any of it specialized.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: It was everybody had the same training pretty much?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, just in different groups. You would have, in other words, a platoon commander, and he had two assistants. And they would take you in groups. And then each one of the assistants would appoint someone that was good in the marching field to be his assistant. So when you broke it down, you actually had four over you.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Well, now, what were the barracks like, the accommodations?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, just double bunks up and down. And you had this little thin mattress about four inches thick, which is part of the sea bag. In other words, when they issue you the clothes, you get them all at one time, including the mattress and a pillow. And then the first step you had to learn was how to lash that up, what they call sea-going fashion. And it weighed 60 pounds.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And they taught you to do that?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, you had to. And you had to roll your clothes. There weren't any clothes hangers. You had to roll them, and you had to cut these little lines and tie them on each end or whatever tie it took.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You didn't have a footlocker for your personal belongings?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Not in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Not in the Navy, no.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You said you had 12 weeks of basic training?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What have we omitted from the basic training. What else did you do? You had weapon training also, did you not?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Your gun training and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. See, you had so many days of each category. And then one of the--really we wasn't supposed to do but eight weeks. But they came and, see, I guess they foresaw what might be ahead of us. We had to go through an additional four weeks, and that was just obstacle training.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Obstacle?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, courses, you know. In other words it would be like a stream of water here. They had to pour diesel fuel on it and light it up. And then you would have like a Jacob's ladder going across that stream. You had to run up here to get a hold of that.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And get over it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: And then another one was that they had had like a tunnel built, and they put gas in it, you know.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you have a gas mask on?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's what I was going to tell you. See, you had to put a gas mask on, but you had to put it on inside of the tunnel. You had to learn how to put it on.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: In the dark.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, see, you had been fitted out with what size. They had the size according to your facial features. But what they would do then, you had to start into this thing, and it was all categories. And then you get so far in there. And they would shoot the gas to it. And that gas smelled just like green corn. I will never forget it. It smelled just like you were down in the cornfield. That's what it smelled like. I will never forget that. And then before you got too deep in there, they would let you put your gas mask on. But you had to run out and put that on in the midst of that. And then the other thing they had in that training was going up a ladder like the side of a ship with your whole sea-bag pack on. You walked with your feet in it and your hands.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: They showed you how to do it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, and there was other things in there. We won't go into detail. There were a lot of little things. For instance, you had to go overboard when your ship got hit and you didn't have a life jacket. We would learn how to wear a shirt with no holes. And you'd take that shirt and button it up and take it off, tie knots in the sleeve. You could sling that and get air in it, and that helped you stay up like a life jacket.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, this is very basic, but since you were in the Navy, I'm sure they gave you swimming lessons right from the start?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Everybody had to be able to swim. We had three in our platoon who couldn't swim. And they asked for volunteers from our men to take the three men and try to teach them, if nothing else, dog-paddling, to stay above water. And I volunteered for that.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Of course, you were close to the river up here.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I learned to swim in that river creek down there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You grew up right near the river so you knew how to swimn.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: And we done it in the skinny.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: There's a lot of other stuff in that obstacle training course. You had to do a lot of jumping and things. We won't go into detail on that.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you have any other people from the Catawba area or from Catawba County that you met while you were in basic training?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, just what I met on the train in Shelby, Walker. He was from Shelby. But after we got out of training, I didn't have any more contact with him.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: He probably moved into a different branch or whatever?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: You get assigned to different areas.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So what happens after basic training?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, they had a unit called Unit D. That's an outgoing unit where they assigned you to a ship, or you might be able to go to school at that time. But during the war, it's hard to get as it is special. But very few men got go to school during the war. But anyhow they had a sign in what we called the outgoing unit. They were opening up a new galley for the men who wanted to get into food service. If you did, you dropped your name in the box. The guy above me, one other young man and I put our names in the box. The next day they took us up to this new galley in Norfolk on the base. But it wasn't in the training end of it. That was where they fed the outgoing units. But anyway there was a new one. That was where they tried you to see if you might want to get in food service.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. In other words, you had choices at that point?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, at that time, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you volunteered for this.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, I volunteered for that and didn't dream about getting it, but I did. I got to stay there a couple of years, two years. I was accepted.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So what ship were you assigned to then?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I was there two years, and I had got up to E-4 petty officer. And then I requested sea duty because I knew that they cut your time just in half between ranks. Do you see what I mean? So I requested sea duty. And then I got assigned to a destroyer being built in San Francisco at Bethlehem Steel. And it was a new one. In other words, that made me what you call a "plank order" on it. They assigned a third of the regular Navy, and then the other two-thirds of the crew were in training to come aboard there. Well, that's a third of the crew they called the original plank owner. Mine was to get all of the food stocked.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Get the supplies?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, you know, before you get ready for the shake-down crew.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, this ship was being built in San Francisco. So you had to go from Norfolk to San Francisco? Or did the ship come to Norfolk?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. We went from Norfolk by train to there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Lets back up a little bit. You were in Norfolk, and you were assigned to food service. And you volunteered to go to sea?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what would have happened had you not gone to sea?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: They would automatically have sent me.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: At some point in time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. After two years, really two years was the normal tour of duty.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But they would have used you in some capacity in Norfolk until they would have assigned you--

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: --before you volunteered to go on this one. So the three of you kind of hung together?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, we didn't. Just I, myself.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You were the only one that got to go to San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: On that ship. And then when I got in the receiving station at Vallejo, California, we were staying there while the ship was finishing being built. We had to go there each day by bus to go aboard. In other words, they hadn't even got it finished, everything done on it. We started stocking stores, or I did. And the other men, like torpedoes and gunners, were stocking theirs.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What was the name of this destroyer?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: USS Gendreau 639, the hull number.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. So how long did it take you to cross the continent to go from Norfolk by train to San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Six days.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Six days?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I remember that well.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But you had sleeping berths and so forth, did you? Or did you have to sleep sitting up?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: You slept in the seat you were sitting in.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That's a long time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But you got to see a lot of the country?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you go through Chicago or the southern route?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, Chicago, you got two changes in there. And then you got to go--I remember going through the Great Salt Flats in Utah. That was something to see. It was in the wintertime too.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You got to see all that salt, the salted flats, and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Tell was happened before you went on your maiden voyage or journey.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: For the life of me, I can't remember the month we got out of there. You are talking about when the ship got ready to go to sea?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: When everything was done and you got everything stocked, the ship, they took the ship to what they call the degaussing unit. What that is, don't ask me about the fluids and stuff that's in it, but it tests that ship for a lightening hit. We would have lightning rods on it, and they got a degaussing unit. And if there is something wrong, they find the detection in there. And they had to take that ship back in the dry dock check out the degaussing, what they call a degaussing unit. Don't ask me what it is. I don't know what it is.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: In other words, you made some trial runs here?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What they call a shakedown. We went from San Francisco to San Diego, and then we went from San Diego. We had to be assigned. We hadn't gotten assigned to the fleet or particular unit like the 7th fleet or Task Force 58. But anyway they sent from us San Diego then to Honolulu, Pearl Harbor. So there we got assigned then to Task Force 58.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. Let's go on the shakedown cruise. You are going from San Francisco to San Diego. You dock there, and you guys get some shore leave?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Some of the men could, but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But the galley you had to watch all that food and all the supplies?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I didn't want to cross country again.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And then you went to Honolulu?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you had shore leave there?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, from 4 p.m. to 12 a.m. Simpack Pacific was the headquarters that assigned the ships to different parts of the fleet in the Pacific. And we got assigned to Task Force 58A.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what was your particular assignment?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Cooking, butchering and baking.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: I'm saying of this--

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, are you talking about the ship's assignment?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Yes

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We got assigned to Task Force 58A, and then we headed to the South Pacific and our first invasion--

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what year are we talking about now?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: '44. So actually you joined in '41, and so you spent quite a bit of time getting ready for the shakedown crews?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you took a lot of training, I guess, in supervising the galley and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And so it's 1944, and you are in Honolulu. And you are headed for the South Pacific?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Tell us about that.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, when we left, we got assigned to Task Force 58, our first invasion was in the area of Marshal Islands. And then we headed on to Guadalcanal out in Tulagi and did a lot of training. And then we left there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Let's talk about the training in Guadalcanal. What kind of training did you receive?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What you did there was mainly gun firing. See, we were what they called an AA type of destroyer.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Explain what an AA destroyer is.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Antiaircraft.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Antiaircraft.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: In other words, we were equipped with the type of guns that were noted to knock planes down. And then we had sonar equipment to detect submarines. We carried torpedoes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: For the submarines.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. And then they carried ash cans, in other words, depth charges. We had what they called full racks of those, which was ten charges that you could fire at one time. You had four in port and four starboard and two big ones, 700-pounders, on the fantail. And these other ones were teardrop-type depth chargers. You go like this. And the other ones just roll off, and you set your detonator for so deep, in other words, like shallow, medium or deep. But you had numbers to go by, and you got your headphones on, and our sonar man detected them.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: He would communicate?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: See, you start heading over it and do what they call laying a pattern. But before we started over where their contact was, we also had another detection unit called hedgehogs. It had 12 of those. They're mounted forward of the bridge. You fire them off first. If they started popping, then you knew it's a metal object down there. So then we would make a run across it and drop what they call run of depth charges, which is ten charges, fire off eight of the tear drops and two of the heavy canisters.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Shake the boat up a little bit?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, how large a crew did you have on the destroyer?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: How large a crew did you have at the destroyer?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We ranged from 280 to 300. It all depended on the ones that was being transferred and what have you, rotations.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What kind of crew did you have on the galley?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I had five cooks besides myself.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So there were six cooks?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And tell us a typical day of what you guys were doing when you were on training in Guadalcanal. What time did you get up in the morning?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Are you talking about in Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: While you were doing training.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I got up between 3:30 a.m. and 4 a.m. We had regular meals, a regular routine what they called "plan of the day." It's written up for the next day.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Let's go with you. Let's run you through a regular day. What time did you get up in the morning?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: If you got the morning watch to cook breakfast, you would be getting up at 3:30 or quarter to 4:00. You feed the crew that's getting ready to go on watch to relieve the ones that's on watch, so you can feed them at 6:00. Then you go from there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: All right. And you prepared two meals, one for the regular crew and one for the officers?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, no. The officers had their own cook.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: They had their own cook?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: He was the head cook in the galley in there with us. But he just had a space where he worked, and he used the same equipment we used.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And how many people did he feed, the officers?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, let's see. There were gunnery officers, two engineer officers, exec, the old man, the sound alarm man, the gunner. I'm going to say about eight.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Now, I'm not positive, but that changed occasionally. Back in those days we had what we called a crypto board, and some of the men came aboard temporarily.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: It varied?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: They wanted to try to break the codes of the Japanese before an invasion.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And then did you do your own cleanup? Or did you have cleanup crews?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, you were it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That was it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Kind of like we used to kid about.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you guys were six cooks, and you had to feed all the rest of the people onboard?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. One of the cooks just baked all of the time.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And then all of the time you cleaned up after breakfast?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. Six mess cooks cleaned up. I did all of the butchering.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, I started out butchering and then worked on up.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you enjoyed that, I take it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So breakfast then and you had to fix lunch, of course.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Lunch was at 12:00, but what you did, you had to start preparing after breakfast because, like I say, if you're planning a roast beef dinner, you know how long it takes to cook that. You had to time it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, who decided on the the menus? Or did they decide? Or did they hand you the menus and say, this is what you are going to make?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, to start with on there, we had this one man that made them out. And then later I got my rank up another step to E-5. And then I was put in charge of doing that, and from then on, you know, I did it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You made sure they bought some persimmon pudding from Catawba in for Thanksgiving and Christmas, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, one outstanding thing was the skipper on there, our first skipper, the commanding office, he was a damn good man, big man and well trained. He had been in combat before. He got command of the ship. But that was his first command as a captain of the ship. But anyway I hadn't took over too long on there planning the menus. You had to have your menu for a full week. And I would have to have that ready.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: For his approval?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Right, that's it. By Friday for next week. And then he would either approve or disapprove of it and send it back down, and then you go from there. But anyway I hadn't been in charge of it too long, and he was down there in the galley. And he'd come around and talk with you. That's another thing I liked about him. A lot of them wouldn't talk to enlisted men unless they really wanted to know something. And don't ever tell them everything. Hold a little back. That's no kidding. No truer words were spoken because he will be wanting to really take over from you. Now, he was in there. We was down in the galley one day. And he said, "Spencer, I want to ask you something." I said, "Yeah." He said, "Why do you have chicken on the menu every Sunday?" I said, "Well, Captain, I was raised on a farm, and that was Sunday dinner."

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: While you were at church, the chicken was baking in the oven, right?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. He said, "You can't beat that." He said, "I just wondered why you didn't put it on some other day. There's nothing wrong with that." I said, "Well, it's just a force of habit."

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: I expect you had a lot of Catholic servicemen, and they would have fish on Friday?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: On Friday we also fish, but I also had another dish with it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You had a choice?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: But it would be like a stew or a meatloaf. It wouldn't be no steak or roast to go along with the fish. But, you know, they stopped that in '45. But I still did it. Later on I made a career in it, and I would still do it just for them. In other words, it didn't cost any more.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: We have got you at Guadalcanal. Where do you go from there?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I headed north into the Pacific. Well, at the end of the war, we got assigned as we went north. We finally got to Okinawa and the invasion there. That was it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what year was that then?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: '45. And one of the few times the main invasion there in Naha, that's one of the big cities in Okinawa. We went in there, did our main bombing and our main shelling and landed troops. It fell on April Fool's Day and Easter Sunday fell on the 1st, you know, April Fool's Day quite a few times. That's why I can remember that one that well.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So did you encounter a lot of resistance.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, Lord, that was the hardest one.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. In Okinawa you were still in training. You hadn't engaged the enemy at that point in time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's what we were doing.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: I'm sorry. Guadalcanal you hadn't engaged any.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. We left there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So Okinawa was the first time you encountered war?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. There were small islands. Well, the one there at Okinawa, that was a hard one to secure, you know. See, we went in there on April 1st, and then the war wasn't over until August 13--I believe that was right--of '45. We got hit. What it was, after the invasion a week or so later the Japs came in and landed on the south side of Okinawa. And we had to go escort some more troops and ST in behind them where they had already gone into the shore. So while we were there, as we went in, why, see, there was a destroyer, a small one, you go in first and close to the beach, and then make your turn. And then these enlistees, other troops, they follow you in. But what I was going to say is we got in there to make the turn and those Japs had guns back in the hills, the mountains and had them on tracks. They had rolled out, and Lord they fired on us, hit us, number 1 fire. And we were dead in the water there for about seven minutes. We got number 2 fire room and number 2 engine room back in, and, you know went on from there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you suffer a lot of casualties?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, we were lucky. We lost--I'm not sure whether this one man died later or not. But I know we lost three firemen in that engine room. See, if they had been a little earlier, they would have gotten eight. But there was one guy, I remember him coming up this hatch, and I could see he was all messed up in front. But I don't know whether he lived or died. But three of them were buried there in Okinawa. We put them in tarps, like buried at sea fashion.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you have any resistance from the air?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, full of it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Full of it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, we got credit for seven planes up to that point.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Your antiaircraft?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's all we got credit for, you know, on that destroyer.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: How about submarines? Did he encounter submarines?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. We got credit for one. But now here I will tell this. It's the truth. What they said about your destroyer was if I was on one and you were on this one, and you are both firing on the same plane, and you knock him down, and you don't know which one got it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you both take credit?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Both. The same way with the submarine. We laid a pattern and destroyed that pattern. We got the submarine. But now each one got, in other words, like I say, it was like North Carolina, you see all these flags up there for a plane, well, they may not have shot all them down, but they fired.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And how long did this warfare last in Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: How long was the battle in Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: See, the invasion began on Easter Sunday and April Fool's Day.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. Tell us when you heard about the war being over.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Back here on leave.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, you were on leave.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. See, I was on the ship, and there were five of us who didn't take rotation when we could have. After you were on there a year we wanted to get our rank. See, you might be back here on a leave, and you would be free until the next rank and you wouldn't get it. So after the second crew got relieved, and we had a new skipper, he looked at our records and called us five up. And he said, "You're going home for leave now." Well, I was back here when the war was over.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. Tell us, did they fly you back?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, rode a ship.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Rode a ship.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Transport.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: To Honolulu, I expect, and San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, all the way to San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: San Francisco. And then you took the train across country again?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That took quite a while then. How long were you on leave?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I had 60 days coming.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Two months?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: But that passed away pretty quick.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you were home, and then you heard the news and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, see I had to report back then to Mare Island--not Mare Island but Treasure Island where they reassigned me. I got in there, and I was sent back to the Pacific again. And I got out to Okinawa to go aboard this big salvage tug, the fleet tug.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So from Catawba on your way back from your leave you went to?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Treasure Island.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you went by train again?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: The same route?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes. And Treasure Island, that's where they assign you. I got assigned to a ship called the Tawakoni (ATF 16th). And it was there at Okinawa, so I had to ride ship back to Okinawa. So I got there, and I remember we was going in, what our mission was--

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What kind of a ship was the Tawakoni?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Tawakoni, it's a big heavy fleet tug, and also does salvage work, like pulling ships that had been sunk.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: What kind of a crew, what size crew did it have?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We had 80 men.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Eighty. And you worked in the galley again?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I was in charge. I had my own men.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And how many people worked under you in the galley?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Two and one baker.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Do you believe it, two people cooking for 80 people three meals a day?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Do you believe it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, it's just one of those things. But we had the equipment.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You had big equipment. Who peeled the potatoes? You guys did?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We had mess men. We called them mess cooks in the Navy, like Army KP. What I was going to say, I remember we pulled in there in '45, and I remember cooking Thanksgiving dinner in Tokyo Bay.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Turkey and dressing?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. It was big really. I could carry a lot of storage. And we were in there in June with two other ones clearing Tokyo Bay and Yokosuka Bay so the ship could get in.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Well, now were you afraid of mines and so forth? Or did they have a mine destroyer kind of clearing it before you guys came?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: The mine sweep had already been there. But now in the bay itself it hadn't, but they had swept everything up to there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: So we had a sonar detector on this one. We could tell. We had a man all the time on that bugger.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you had some big cranes on the ship too, I guess?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, well, yeah, booms, the kind, you know, out and had a tooling engine, and we had a four-inch cable we could pull with.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Pretty heavy stuff?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We tied the open end dry dock all the way from outside of Okinawa all the way back to the States whenever we came back.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, how long were you on this ship?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I was on there about eight months, and I got off that ship in July, late July of '46. We got back to the States.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Back to San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, actually Graham Shipyards in Oakland.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oakland. It's in the same area.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Just across the bay, San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Then you had some shore leave and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, came back and got married.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Really. California girl?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. I came back by train again. I had 60 days I could still get. And I came home back and got married.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, she was from Catawba?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, we were classmates in school together, first grade through the eleventh.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you corresponded, I guess, during the war and all that?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Some, not too heavy. There wasn't much you could write during the war.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: They censored it?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: They cut it out.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what was her name?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Margie Dale Stewart.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Margie Dale Stewart.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So that was a nice homecoming for you?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Bu then you had to go back?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did she go back with you?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes. And we had to report to the nearest duty assignment station, which was Norfolk. So I had bought an old car while I was here. It was hard to get cars then. I bought one from Buddy Body Works in Hickory. My brother had located them up there. They had a '42 Dodge, and they had a '42 Dodge coupe. And they had a '42 Ford sedan. And I bought that Dodge. Guess what I paid him for it?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Through the nose, 14 big ones.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That was a lot of money back then.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What are you talking about. But it paid off. I tell you about that later maybe.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you drove it to Norfolk from here.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That was the nearest place to get reassigned. Well, we got to Norfolk and got in there and had to stay. They had two good hotels there, two nice ones. But the Monticello was real expensive, and then they had one called the Atlantic. And so we stayed in it, but it wasn't too hot. It had a few bugs in it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, dear.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She saw those. And the next morning she said, "We have to get out to that base for you to get reassigned, and you try to find somebody to get us the hell out of Norfolk."

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: She didn't like Norfolk, the bugs in Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Everything about it she didn't like. So we got out to the base, and I got in there. I went up there to the receiving station headquarters. I had gotten up to E-6 petty officer, which is a good rank. I got to looking around in that office to see if I could recognize any faces to help me out, you know, to get me away from Norfolk. And lo and behold there was one officer in here. He and I were together in a galley. And he was the ex-storekeeper. He went from storekeeper and went on up, passed the enlisted rank and got the ward officer. And he was in charge of assignments. Luckily, the good Lord was with me there. I asked him, "Lee,"--(I didn't call him Mister)--"I need some help." He said, "Do you want to get paid?" I said, "That's one of them." And I said, "I got another request. Can you get me back to the West Coast?" He said, "You're wanting a pretty big order." He said, "Go in there and sit down." He had to go over to his desk. He said, "It will take me about 30 minutes, and I'll see what's open for the West Coast." Ordinarily you would have to stay there. But he said, "I've got friends out there." And there is Goat Island. That's another receiving station for reassignments. They're in San Francisco. He said, "I tried Treasure Island and couldn't find anybody. But," he said, "I got in Goat Island. I got in contact with another officer." He said, "I got you signed orders to Goat Island. And he'll get you set for something in the Pacific" because I wanted to go back to the Pacific. Lo and behold I got in there. He fixed me up.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you travel with car across the country?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Drove across the country. I took the old car and made it.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You took the Dodge?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, I took the Dodge and my wife. And there he got me assigned to the submarine auxiliary base, and we were on an island in the Philippines. So I was there. I was there just about a year or so. And then we got orders to decommission the base, and I got reassigned to Subbase Pearl. The old man called us up. And all E-6s and E-7s had put a request in for two commands, and he said he would try to get us one of them. And that was good of him. For he liked the work that we had done. And I requested submarine tender Nerevs. But I didn't get it. Then the next one I put in for any base in the Pacific. And I got assigned to Luzan Island auxiliary base. But anyways, after that the old man got the orders. He got me a set of orders. I got to go to Subbase Pearl, and we got in there in late '47.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Now, Pearl being Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, submarine base there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: In Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, in Hawaii. Best duty I ever had.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And your wife was there, of course?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, not there. Later.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: She came later, I guess.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She came a little later.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: But she was still in San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She had already come back home.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Oh, she went back home by that time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes. Then I flew home in January of '48. I flew from San Francisco and picked her up and got the old Dodge and back we went.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Across country again?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, and got there and I had to report to Mare Island. That's where you got transporation. See, they had the submarine base there, you know. They went back to Pearl. Well, I had to go on by a ship back to Pearl. Before I left for Pearl, I took my car to Oakland to be transported to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: The car was waiting for you when you were there?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, lucky. And then when I got there, I called Margie. And she flew out on Pan Am. I had been on the housing waiting list long enough so we had an apartment when she arrived.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Well, did she like Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She hated to leave. I got to stay there better than three years. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what kind of work did you do while you were stationed there?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I was what they call a galley captain. I was in charge. I hadn't been promoted to the rank of chief yet, but there was a chief over me, and I was assistant over everything.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You were next in command?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, second in command.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: How many people worked in the galley at that point in time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We usually had about 28.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And how large a crew?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: When we ranged 600 or 700, it varied. See, it was like a receiving station, men coming off of subs in transit and so on.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: A lot of food to prepare?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: I tell you better than that. I will tell you one better than that in a little bit. Then I got an extension there for a third year. The third year got up, and I got a little more time there. But then I got assigned to the Helena, heavy gun cruiser in '51, April of '51.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Helena, that was a heavy cruiser?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yes, CA75. And I had no more than gotten aboard there, we got away from the dock, and we headed to Korea. So we got up there then, and we were in two invasions up there. The first one one was Wonsan Harbor.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And this has to be what? 1951 at that time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, '51.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: So you were in Korea also?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. And then in the Wonsan Harbor we got hit, They fired on us. And what it was, Wonsan Harbor is like a horseshoe. And, see, 8-inch guns could fire accurately at 8 miles. But anything further could go as far as ten miles, but it's not accurate. But anyway we were firing off right at the edge of the harbor going into Wonsan. And we were missing our target. We had a lot of commandos spotting for it, plus our own helicopter. Well, we were falling short. And we were the flagship for the Korean task force. We had Admiral Libby, vice admiral. Anyway, he and the old man got together. They decided to pull in. We pulled in all right. And we no more than got in there and we started firing, we were hitting our target. But one of their guns hit us in the fantail down where the helicopter pad was.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Any casualties?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We were lucky. There was nobody there. The helicopter saw his crew. The helicopter was in the air, and his crew had gone forward. And when you're firing in combat, you stay away from those 8-inch guns. You've got to get inside, and so they went forward. But like I say, we were real lucky there. We didn't lose anyone.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And what damage was done to your cruiser?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: After that we had to come back to Tokyo, Japan.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Dry dock?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Not dry yet. They could do it. They could do it while we were afloat. They patched us up. And when they got through cutting it out to put the deck back down, see, you have a steel deck and then you have a wooden deck on top of that in the heavy cruiser and battle wagon. Well, they had to cut a hole there, 18 by 36, to get it where they could patch it good. That's how much it was torn up back there. Then we went back up to Korea.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did did you take on water as a result of that?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, huh-uh, we were lucky. It was a super-structure deck. But anyhow we left after we got patched up in Tokyo. We went back up and went to Songrim. That was our next invasion.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That's in Korea also.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's in the northern part. And there was a funny thing. They were using them B29s to bomb, but you had certain targets. You see you had on your charts certain targets. You could hit, and you couldn't bomb. I can see them yet, those 29s coming across. They would start their pattern. Once you started a pattern to bomb, you can't stop it. The whole shoot has to go out. Well, they came across and hit their target. And then they would pull out over the ocean. And then we're out here. Of course, now, we had other ships with us. We had a sister ship. But we were also in that invasion. And we shelled a lot of bridges. They got a lot of trains up and down the coast. And that was it. Then I got shore duty. It had been closed. But I had sea duty. And overseas I had enough time built up that I could request shore duty.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And went back to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: No, I came back and requested San Diego.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: San Diego. So your wife in the meantime--

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She was at Pearl, while I was aboard the Helena. When I got orders to go to San Diego--

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: She joined you there that?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: She had to pack our furniture. She joined me down there. I went to the Naval Training Center in San Diego. And there I got placed in charge of the cold storage building.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And tell us about your duties there.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, what that was was this cold storage building, with all the food, they were feeding 21,000 in there at that time when I first got there. It fluctuated between 21 to 23 all depending on how the platoons broke. Anyway, the cold storage building there was where all the food was shipped in, and then we issued it out to the different ships.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You were a warehouse basically?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's what it amounted to, a warehouse, cold storage.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And they ordered food from you, and you had to make sure?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. See, if you were in charge of food service in this galley, you would send me up what you needed in the vegetables and what you needed, period.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you deal with frozen food at that time also?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Did you deal with frozen food at that time?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we had a lot of that.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And a lot of fresh produce, I guess?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Both, yeah, we had both, a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Canned goods and everything else?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: We didn't have it. There was another warehouse.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That was different. You dealt with cold storage?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Refrigerated.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Eggs and so forth?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Eggs.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Dressed chickens and so forth, meat?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Sides of beef.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: See, that was your area.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: There were sides too, like fore quarters, hind quarters. They came in these trailers. They hung them.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: On hooks. They came from Omaha, I guess?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you about that. King Packing, King Ranch was the largest ranch here in the States. Our eggs came in crates of 32 dozen from Norfolk, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: By train, I guess.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Okay. So you are in San Diego.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah, I stayed there two years. It was time for reassignment again, so I had to call.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Call your friend again?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Well, I better say this, whether it's on tape or not, it doesn't make any difference. There's a little politics in the service. Don't let anybody kid you. If you've been with a certain command and you were a certain rank, but higher than me, and if you and I got along good and later you got command of a station or ship, (if you liked me), I could pull your leg.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: So that's what I had to do whenever I got ready to leave San Diego. My wife said, "What are you going to do. Take your chance on the receiving station? Or are you going to call your friend? I had a friend by the name of Gulard (spelling) and he was the next man that had been working like the storekeeper. But Gulard had got up to the rank of lieutenant, full lieutenant. I said, "Lord, I am going to call Gulard." So one evening I called him. And he said, "Well, give me until tomorrow. I got to check things out and see." There has to be an opening.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: They can't create openings?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: There has to be an opening for your rank. So he said, "Give me until tomorrow. I will find you a slot. I'll try to get you a good one." The next day he called us, and Margie answered the phone. And I saw her get a frown on her face, and I didn't know what he said to her. And then after a while she started laughing. They talked a little while. And then she said, Hal wants to talk to you." I talked to him. He said, "Margie didn't faint, did she?" I said, "No." He said, "Well, I told her you were going to go to Alaska in the commissary store up there. And then I told her you are going to the nearest submarine sitting out there in the bay in San Diego, the S14." Yeah. So I got aboard it, went aboard it and stayed there three years.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: Submarine base?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Submarine tender. San Diego isn't a submarine base. We had two tenders down there.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And you had served in one previously, of course?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Yeah. And I was getting back up in the submarine force. And anyway I got to stay over three years. And then time got up again for another assignment. And she asked me again, "Well, what are you going to do?" I said, "Call Gulard." So we did. And the same thing, wait a day. And the next day he called, and he used that same story.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: The Alaska story?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: And called in charge of the commissary store, but she didn't believe him that time. He said, "No. You are going on the Pelias (AS14). That was another submarine tender in Mare Island. So I got to stay aboard there three years, and I got a year extension. And then when that's up, I didn't know where I was going. But I pulled a leg again, and I got an assignment on a field food service team. The Navy had two west of the Mississippi and two east of the Mississippi. And our primary duties were, say you were the commanding officer of this ship here and maybe you think that your mess men in the food service could stand some help improving maybe with new ideas.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You are doing consulting and training?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: That's what it amounted to. But we already had to have certain schools, which I had been to the Class B schools. That sound like a second grade school. But Class B in San Diego was the top school in food service. And then we did a lot of testing on different dishes. And then the latest thing that might be on the market, we combined into a menu.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: And new equipment, I expect?

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Right. Well, the whole works.

sp.speaker: Sidney Halma
sp.p: You are the authorities on food.

sp.speaker: Vernon A. Spencer
sp.p: Supposed to be kind of outstanding. Well, you had to have certain school and stuff to get to be a member of that team. Well, we got on that. And I still went to Alaska though. We flew up there. Yeah, went up there on one of our tours and made the Alaskan chain. We went out to Kodiak, Cold Bay, Adak and Shemya. See, Shemya is right there again on the Russian border, a big fence and communication stations are there. The Russians have got one, and we've got one. And then in Kodiak we have planes, patrol planes, that patrol that whole area up there. Upon retiring from the military, for several years I managed three restaurants, two in Iredell County and one in Catawba County.
